analysis.one_liner: Pays hospital-owned off-campus clinics at the lower doctor-office rate instead of the higher hospital rate.
analysis.headline: The bill to stop hospitals billing off-campus clinics at higher hospital rates never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When hospitals buy doctor practices and clinics that sit away from the main hospital, Medicare currently pays for the same service at a much higher "hospital rate" than it would in an ordinary doctor's office. This bill would close those exceptions and require the clinics to bill under their own separate identifier, so insurers can tell what was actually done and where. It would also let private insurers reject claims that hospitals bill improperly for off-campus services.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare patients and taxpayers would gain: the same service done in a hospital-owned clinic off the hospital campus would be paid at the lower rate used for doctor offices, which would lower Medicare spending and the share of it patients pay out of pocket (copays and deductibles are a percentage of what Medicare allows). People with private insurance would also gain, because the bill would bar hospitals from billing a clinic visit under the hospital's identity and from holding the patient liable for a claim billed that way.

how_it_helps.text: It removes the exceptions that let hospital-owned clinics off the main campus be paid at the full hospital rate, so the same service is paid at the lower doctor-office rate, lowering Medicare costs and patients' percentage-based copays.
It requires each off-campus clinic to have its own unique billing identifier and to bill on the standard physician form, so hospitals cannot make a clinic visit look like a hospital service.

It bars hospitals from billing a private insurer for off-campus services under the hospital's identity, and from holding the patient liable for such a claim, and asks the state insurance regulators' association to write model rules letting insurers reject improperly billed claims, modeled on Colorado House Bill 18-1282.

It adds explicit authority for the Health and Human Services Secretary to adopt site-neutral payment policies to prevent hospitals from billing off-campus clinic services as if they were furnished at the hospital.

analysis.who_pays: Hospital systems that own off-campus clinics would bear the cost: they would no longer collect the higher "hospital rate" for services performed in those clinics, and they would need new billing identifiers and forms. Part of that cost could show up as lower revenue that hospitals say helps fund emergency rooms and other money-losing services.

drawbacks.text: Hospitals argue the higher off-campus payments help cover emergency rooms, trauma care, and other unprofitable services, so site-neutral payment could squeeze rural and safety-net hospitals and push some clinics to close or be sold, reducing access for some patients.
The bill's benefit to patients depends on insurers and Medicare actually passing savings through as lower copays and premiums rather than keeping them, which the bill does not guarantee.
The compliance deadline was written as January 1, 2024 for a bill introduced in April 2023 that never advanced, leaving providers an unrealistic transition window had it passed later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its face the trade is favorable: Medicare pays roughly twice as much for the same service at a hospital-owned off-campus clinic as at a doctor's office, and patients' copays scale with that inflated amount, so closing the gap saves taxpayers and patients money with little change in care delivered. The real costs fall on hospitals, some of which legitimately use those margins to subsidize emergency and charity care, and a bill this narrow does nothing to offset that. But those trade-offs were never litigated, because the bill never received so much as a hearing; the outcome for the public was not a considered rejection of the policy, it was inaction.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and their Health Subcommittee for the whole Congress without ever getting a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 25, 2023 and referred to two committees, Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means.
It was sent to the Health Subcommittee on April 28, 2023, and the referral was renewed on December 17, 2024, but no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee, so all its provisions expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospital systems that bill services at off-campus clinics under the higher hospital rate are better off, since the change never happened. Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers are no better off than before, and the overbilling it targeted continued through the 118th Congress.

industries.industry: Hospital systems (especially those that acquire physician practices)
industries.note: Hospital systems earn more by paying doctors' salaries and billing their work at the higher hospital rate; this bill would strip that premium for off-campus clinics and require separate billing identifiers that make the practice visible to insurers. Congress's inaction preserved that revenue stream.

industries.industry: Private health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: Insurers and group health plans would gain a federal right to reject claims for off-campus services billed under the hospital's identity, a step toward the protections Colorado adopted in House Bill 18-1282, which the bill directs the NAIC to model.
Medicare Advantage plans fall under the new billing requirements, so they too could see claims come in with the correct clinic-level identifier rather than the hospital's.
